dataset.what_one_row_represents: A single orbital launch attempt (success or failure) catalogued in Jonathan McDowell's JSR Launch Vehicle Database.
dataset.time_range: 1957-10-04 to 2018-10 (Sputnik through October 2018; the final year is incomplete)
dataset.geographic_scope: Global. 17 distinct state_code values; the agencies CSV carries lat/long for sites but ~half are missing or set to '-'.

ana_00.label: Dataset shape
ana_00.content: The launches table holds 5,726 rows and 11 columns spanning 1957 to 2018. There are 40 distinct launching agencies and 17 state_codes; agency_type is fully populated (no missing values). The companion agencies table has 74 rows describing each launch provider's metadata.

ana_01.label: Yearly global launches 1957-2018
ana_01.content: Global orbital launch cadence climbed from 3 attempts in 1957 to a peak of 139 in 1967, hovered near the 100-130/year mark through the late Cold War, then collapsed after 1991 — bottoming out at just 53 launches in 2004. The 2010s show a recovery to roughly 80-90/year. The 2018 figure of 80 is partial: data only runs through October.

calculation.output:
PEAK: 1967 with 139 launches
POST-1965 TROUGH: 2004 with 53 launches
2018 (partial): 80
1957: 3

ana_02.label: Yearly launches by bloc — the great inversion
ana_02.content: Splitting launches by bloc shows the Cold War duopoly turning inside out. The USSR led every year from 1967 to 1991, peaking at 108 launches in 1982 — more than four times its US rival that year. Russia's inheritance of the Soviet program then declined, falling from 91 in 1991 to just 10 in 2018. Meanwhile China rose from a single launch in 1970 to 28 in 2018, surpassing both Russia and the United States in cadence. By 2018 the order is China (28), the United States (27), the 'Other' bloc (15) — and Russia, the original space leader, last at 10.

calculation.output:
1957:    SU=2 US=1 CN=0 Other=0
1982:    SU=108 US=18 CN=1 Other=2
1991:    SU=61 US=19 CN=1 Other=10
2018:    RU=10 US=27 CN=28 Other=15

data_table.description: Launches per year by bloc (USSR/Russia treated as a continuous lineage)

ana_03.label: Soviet peak vs. Russian collapse vs. China's rise
ana_03.content: The Soviet Union's launch peak was 108 in 1982 — a cadence the United States never matched in any single year (the US peak was 77 in 1966). By 2018 Russia, the inheritor of Soviet capability, conducted only 10 launches: barely 9% of its 1982 high. China's trajectory ran the other way, from 5 launches in 1990 to 28 in 2018.

ana_04.label: agency_type breakdown all-time
ana_04.content: Across 5,726 launches, 83.4% were conducted by state agencies (4,776), 15.4% by private firms (880), and just 1.2% by startups (70). The state share is dominated by Cold War totals — until 1984 every single launch in the dataset is state-run.

ana_05.label: Yearly launches by agency_type
ana_05.content: The first private launch in the data is in 1984; private operators reach more than half of all launches by 2000. Startups appear only in 2006 (a single Falcon 1 attempt) and stay rare for a decade — then explode: 19 in 2017 and 18 in 2018, more than half of all launches that year coming from companies that did not exist before 2002.

ana_06.label: Top 15 launch providers all-time
ana_06.content: The top of the table is dominated by state codes used as catch-all agencies. The single largest is the US umbrella code (1,202 launches), followed by RU (619) and CN (302). Among named providers, Arianespace ranks first (260), then ILS Khrunichev (97), Mitsubishi/JAXA-era J (78), and ULA-Lockheed (71). SpaceX, founded in 2002, has 68 cumulative launches by October 2018 — the highest count of any firm classified 'startup'.

ana_08.label: SpaceX yearly cadence
ana_08.content: SpaceX flew once in 2006 (Falcon 1), didn't reach 5 launches until 2014, then jumped to 18 in 2017 — the inflection year that crossed it past Arianespace and ULA in annual cadence. By October 2018 the company had flown 17 more, putting cumulative launches at 68.

ana_09.label: SpaceX cumulative trajectory
ana_09.content: Cumulatively, SpaceX reaches 5 launches only by 2009, 25 by the end of 2015 — the year Falcon 9 first landed back on a drone ship — and 68 by October 2018. The slope steepens twice: once after the 2015 land-back demonstration, again after the second-stage manufacturing scale-up in 2017.

ana_10.label: Failure rate by decade
ana_10.content: Orbital launch was wildly dangerous in its first years — 53.8% of attempts failed during 1957-1959. The rate fell sharply with vehicle maturity: 13% in the 1960s, 5% in the 1970s, just under 3% in the 1980s, and 3-5% in every decade since. The 2010s sit at 3.7% — about one in 27 attempts.

ana_11.label: Failure rate by agency type
ana_11.content: Private firms have the lowest failure rate at 2.6% (23/880) — they entered late, with mature vehicle designs and proven engineering. State agencies sit at 6.6% (314/4,776), pulled up by the Cold War's experimental years. Startups, the smallest cohort, have the highest rate at 7.1% (5/70) — a reminder that new vehicles still fail at roughly the historical maiden-flight rate.

ana_12.label: Total launches and overall failure rate
ana_12.content: Across 61 years and 5,726 attempts, 5,384 reached orbit and 342 failed — a cumulative success rate of 94.0%. Failures are heavily front-loaded: roughly half occurred before 1970.

ana_13.label: Synthesised launch-site coordinates (reference layer)
ana_13.content: The agencies CSV's lat/long fields are mostly missing or set to '-' (the dataset's null sentinel). To support a map view, we manually annotate the 19 best-known historical orbital launch sites using their public coordinates — Baikonur (45.96N), Plesetsk (62.93N), Cape Canaveral (28.49N), Kourou (5.22N — the most equatorial), Jiuquan (40.96N), Xichang (28.25N), Tanegashima (30.40N), Sriharikota (13.73N), Sohae (39.66N), and so on. This is reference geography, not a per-launch coordinate join: individual launches in the data do not carry site coordinates.

ana_15.label: Cold War bloc share (1957-1991)
ana_15.content: Through 1991, the USSR and US together carried out 95.6% of every orbital launch attempt — a near-total duopoly. The Soviet bloc alone accounted for 66.7% (2,444 of 3,663). China's share over those 35 years was 0.9%; everyone else combined managed 3.5%.

ana_16.label: Post-Cold War bloc share (1992-2018)
ana_16.content: Since 1992 the picture has flattened dramatically. Russia still leads on cumulative count (35.6%), but only because the 1990s carried over Soviet-era cadence. The United States holds 32.0%, China 13.0%, and 'Other' — Europe, Japan, India, Israel, Iran, and the rest — has climbed to 19.4%. The duopoly is gone.

ana_17.label: Full state_code ranking
ana_17.content: Seventeen distinct launching states appear in the data; just six have launched more than 100 times. The long tail includes Brazil (2), the United Kingdom (2, both Black Arrow), and three South Korean attempts (KR).

ana_19.label: Startup explosion 2017-2018
ana_19.content: The startup category contains exactly two firms in the data — SpaceX and Rocket Lab USA. Together they recorded just 23 launches in their first 11 years (2006-2016), then 19 in 2017 and 18 in 2018. More than half of every startup launch ever recorded happened in the final two years of the dataset.

caveats.content: 2018 data is incomplete — it runs through October only, so all 2018 figures are partial. The dataset's actual final calendar year is therefore smaller than its eventual real-world total.

The agencies CSV stores missing values as the literal string '-' rather than NaN. Latitude/longitude fields are largely either missing or '-'; usable per-launch coordinates are not directly available, so any map of launch sites must be built from external coordinates.
Soviet (SU) and Russian (RU) state codes are treated as a continuous lineage in the bloc views (ana_02, ana_15, ana_16). Without that join, post-1991 totals are split awkwardly across two codes.

The 'agency' column mixes umbrella state-level codes (US, RU, CN, J, IN) with named operators (SpaceX, Arianespace, Mitsubishi, etc.). A row labelled 'US' does not mean a specific firm — it represents a launch attributed to the US national program rather than to a named subsidiary.
The 'startup' agency_type contains only two firms: SpaceX (SPX, 68 launches) and Rocket Lab USA (RLABU, 1 launch). Generalising about 'startups' from this dataset is really generalising about SpaceX.
